action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude a structural, vascular or atypical-parkinsonism cause
action_criteria.rationale: PD is a clinical diagnosis; MRI is normal in PD and excludes vascular lesions, NPH, mass and the midbrain, pontine and putaminal signs of PSP and MSA [Postuma_2015]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Normal cardiac MIBG uptake: early H/M 2.15, delayed H/M 2.02, washout 28%
action_criteria.label: Consider cardiac MIBG scintigraphy
action_criteria.rationale: Cardiac sympathetic innervation is usually preserved in MSA and reduced in PD; a normal study is consistent with preganglionic autonomic failure but does not establish the diagnosis [Wenning_2022]

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Tamsulosin, lisinopril and sildenafil identified as worsening orthostatic hypotension with levodopa; midodrine noted to raise supine pressure

action_criteria.rationale: Tamsulosin, lisinopril and sildenafil each add to the neurogenic orthostatic fall that already caused near-syncope, and any pressor treatment needs supine pressure monitoring [Wenning_2022]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not add drugs that worsen orthostatic hypotension (diuretics, further alpha-blockers or vasodilators)
Do not start an antimuscarinic for the urinary urgency before the post-void residual is known: it worsens incomplete emptying
required_recommendations: Diagnose clinically probable MSA-P (MDS 2022): neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (34/26 mmHg at 1 minute without heart-rate compensation) and parkinsonism, with supportive features of early postural instability with falls and erectile dysfunction before 60, and the MRI marker of putaminal atrophy with signal decrease on iron-sensitive sequences; poor levodopa responsiveness cannot be stated until a trial of up to 1000 mg/day for at least a month [Wenning_2022]
Start a levodopa trial titrated up to 1000 mg/day as tolerated, with lying and standing blood pressure at each step [Wenning_2022]

Treat the neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: review the need for tamsulosin, daytime lisinopril and sildenafil; non-pharmacological measures (fluids and salt, head-up tilt of the bed, compression garments, slow rising, smaller meals); and consider midodrine or droxidopa if symptoms persist, monitoring the supine pressure (142/88 mmHg before treatment)
Measure the post-void residual and assess the bladder before any prostate surgery; intermittent catheterisation if the residual is 100 mL or more
Arrange physiotherapy and fall prevention for the four backward falls, and multidisciplinary follow-up (speech and swallowing, occupational therapy, discussion of prognosis)

interactions: Tamsulosin (alpha-1 blocker) lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further. Review the need for each and measure lying and standing blood pressure at each levodopa dose step.
Lisinopril lowers standing blood pressure and adds to the orthostatic fall; levodopa can lower it further.
Sildenafil adds to hypotension, including orthostatic hypotension.
Polyethylene glycol 3350: no interaction with levodopa.
warnings: Midodrine, if used for orthostatic hypotension, raises supine blood pressure: measure the supine pressure before and during treatment and give the last dose at least 4 hours before lying down.
Antimuscarinic bladder drugs worsen incomplete bladder emptying and add to constipation.
Penicillin allergy recorded: not relevant to the dopaminergic options.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Robert Callahan is a 60-year-old right-handed retired civil engineer who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Karen, for evaluation of progressive motor slowing, gait instability, and recurrent episodes of lightheadedness that have developed over the past eighteen months. His wife first noticed changes approximately eighteen months ago when he began having difficulty keeping pace while walking together on their evening walks, something they had done without issue for years. Over the ensuing months, she observed that his movements became generally slower and more deliberate, affecting activities such as buttoning his shirt, tying his shoes, and cutting food at dinner. He has not noticed a tremor, and his wife concurs that she has not seen a clear resting tremor, though she has observed his hands shake slightly when holding up a newspaper or a cup of coffee. Approximately twelve months ago, he fell backward while stepping off a curb and sustained a minor scalp laceration. Since then, he has had three additional falls, all involving loss of balance in the backward direction, including one episode in which he fell in the shower. His balance difficulties have made him increasingly cautious, and he now uses a handrail whenever available. Concurrently, he has experienced worsening lightheadedness, particularly upon standing from a seated or lying position, and occasionally after meals. Six months ago he nearly lost consciousness while standing in line at the grocery store and was evaluated in urgent care, where orthostatic hypotension was documented. His primary care physician reduced his lisinopril dose from 20 mg to 10 mg, but the lightheadedness has persisted. His wife also reports that he has had increasing difficulty with urinary urgency and has had two urinary tract infections in the past year, which his urologist attributed to incomplete bladder emptying. His chronic constipation, present for approximately four years, has worsened considerably despite daily polyethylene glycol, and he now sometimes goes five to six days without a bowel movement. His erectile dysfunction predates his motor symptoms by approximately one to two years. He denies visual hallucinations, vivid dreams, or acting out dreams during sleep. He reports mild difficulty concentrating when reading but denies significant memory problems. His handwriting has become smaller, which he attributed to rushing. He has not been exposed to neuroleptics, metoclopramide, or other dopamine-blocking agents. He has no history of encephalitis, head trauma, or toxic exposures. His mother has a longstanding essential tremor, but there is no family history of parkinsonism or ataxia.

neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact at great toes bilaterally. Vibration sense intact. No sensory level. Romberg positive with notable postural sway.
